We were to make for the survey camp at first light. I had wanted to press on, for the air was unnervingly clear and the ice-field ahead looked, in the deceptive twilight, as solid as granite. The geologist, a man named Hargrove with a face perpetually pinched by a private anxiety, thought otherwise. He insisted the pressure ridges were treacherous after sundown, that what looked like solid ground could be a thin crust over the grinding chaos of the floe. Moreover, he argued, the forecast promised a deep freeze by morning, which would fix the ice in place and render our passage, if not easy, at least predictable. His reasoning was sound, of course; another ten hours of delay was a small price for the integrity of the traction-sleds. I was nevertheless irritated in the extreme at being frozen in place, a feeling as illogical as it was profound, for what was one more night against the slow eternity of the past year? As we had fuel enough to keep the cabin heaters whining, and prudence was the supreme virtue in this part of the world, I gave the order to power down the drive.

The plain was boundless, a disc of absolute white under a sky of bruised purple. The silence descended not gently, but as a physical weight. The very air, stripped of all moisture by the cold, seemed to have been turned to glass. Each star emerged with a hard, piercing brilliance, not twinkling, but fixed, like the heads of silver nails hammered into a lid of iron. It was not a peaceful silence; it was the silence of a world utterly dead. You could stare out at the blankness until your eyes ached with the effort, and begin to feel your own pulse as a vulgar intrusion, a noisy machine in a vast and sacred tomb. Then the true dark fell, a sudden, sightless void, and you felt the cold not on your skin, but inside your bones.

Sometime near midnight a tremor ran through the sled, a low, resonant vibration that made the metal plates beneath my boots hum. It was followed by a sound, a deep and mournful groaning that seemed to issue from the very bedrock of the planet. It rose in pitch to a prolonged, grating shriek, as if a god were dragging his chains across the floor of the sea. It stopped. A series of percussive cracks, like distant rifle fire, echoed for a moment, and then the crushing silence returned, heavier than before. The sheer alien quality of it made the small hairs on my neck prickle. I do not know how it affected the others; to me it felt as though the ice itself had cried out in agony, a lament that came from everywhere and nowhere at once. The uproar culminated in a final, shattering boom that left us trembling in the sudden quiet, straining our ears against a stillness that was now, somehow, more menacing than the noise. ‘Saints above, what was that?’ whispered one of the surveyors at my shoulder; a gaunt, hollow-eyed man from the low countries who seemed to be in a state of perpetual prayer. Another, a thick-set fellow with a blond beard, simply stood with his mouth agape, his breath pluming in the frigid air like a ghost of a soul departing.

What we could see of our world was just the faint outline of the sled’s housing, its edges softened by a thin frost, and a few yards of flattened snow around it; all else was swallowed by the polar night. The rest of creation had ceased to exist, erased without so much as a whisper of wind. I moved to the forward port and peered into the blackness. ‘Will it hold?’ a fearful voice asked from behind me. ‘The whole sheet could break up,’ muttered another. Their faces were pale masks in the dim cabin light, eyes wide and unblinking. It was a curious thing to see the contrast between these men of science and the local guides we had hired, who were as new to this particular wasteland as we were, though their people had lived on its fringes for a thousand years. The surveyors, of course, were deeply unnerved, and wore a look of personal offence, as if the ice had violated some fundamental contract of physics. The guides, on the other hand, showed a quiet, alert curiosity; but their faces were fundamentally serene, even the one or two who exchanged low, guttural comments that seemed to bring them some measure of understanding. Their leader, an old man with a face like a carved walnut, his eyes nearly lost in a web of wrinkles, stood near the door. ‘An ill sound,’ I said, for the sake of companionship. ‘The ice speaks,’ he replied, his voice a dry rustle, his gaze fixed on the darkness. ‘It is hungry.’ ‘Hungry?’ I asked. ‘What could it eat out here?’ ‘It eats the light,’ he said, without a trace of poetry. ‘It eats the warmth. It eats the noise. Soon it will eat us.’ He adjusted the thick furs on his shoulders and continued to stare out, his posture one of patient and unflinching observance. I should have been chilled by his words, no doubt, had it not struck me that he and his kin were nearly out of provisions. They had been with us for two months, and their notions of time were, I suspect, as abstract as the landscape itself. They belonged to an earlier draft of mankind; they had no ledgers or calendars to measure their own dwindling existence against. So long as a chit was signed in some distant, warm office, it occurred to no one to wonder how they might survive. They had a small supply of dried, oily fish, which was long gone, pilfered by the surveyors who had grown tired of their own canned rations. After that, they were given, each week, a small tin of biscuits and a plug of tobacco; a wage considered more than generous by the company. You can imagine what use that was. There were no trading posts, no settlements, and Hargrove, who like the rest of us ate preserved meats and dehydrated vegetables, would not countenance stopping for the men to hunt, for some obscure reason tied to the expedition’s schedule. So, unless they could smoke the tobacco for nourishment, or build a shelter from biscuit tins, I failed to see how their handsome salary benefited them. Why, in the name of all the hollow devils of starvation, they did not turn on us—they were six to our four—and claim our well-stocked larder, is a mystery to me still. They were hardy men, with a strength forged by generations of hardship, and with little appreciation for the niceties of law. And I saw that some principle of restraint, one of those secrets of the human heart that defy all logic, was at work. I looked at them with a sudden, sharp interest, not because I feared they might butcher me for my share of the beans, though I admit that it was then I noticed, as if for the first time, how soft and fleshy the surveyors appeared, and I hoped, yes, I truly hoped, that my own lean frame was not quite so—what is the word?—so—inviting: a flicker of absurd vanity that suited the waking dream my life had become. Perhaps the cold was getting to me, too. One cannot spend one’s days with a finger pressed constantly to the pulse of one’s own sanity. I had often ‘a touch of the cold,’ or a slight ringing in the ears—the gentle taps of the great white emptiness, the preliminary courtesies before the earnest assault that I knew must come. Yes; I watched them as you would watch any marvel of nature.

Theirs was a stillness not of exhaustion but of profound patience, the patience of stone, of mountains, of things that measure their existence in epochs, not in the frantic ticking of a company-issued chronometer. The surveyors, by contrast, were all nervous energy and fidgeting limbs, their modernity a fragile shell against the immense, ancient cold. They were men built for offices and paved streets, and out here their souls had caught a chill from which they might never recover.

The silence that followed was of a different quality than the one that had preceded the cry. Before, it had been a vacant, listening silence; now it was heavy, glutted, as if it had fed on that sound and was now digesting it in the colossal, unseen stomach of the wilderness. The air itself seemed to have gained weight. Hargrove was the first to stir, clearing his throat with a dry rasp that was shockingly loud. ‘We proceed,’ he announced, his voice straining for a tone of command it could not quite achieve. ‘The schedule, gentlemen. The schedule is paramount.’ It was a faith, you see, this belief in schedules and timetables, a kind of desperate prayer offered up to the god of progress in a land that had never heard its name. One of the surveyors, a young man named Jennings who had a perpetually panicked look, whimpered something about waiting for daylight, for the sun. Hargrove rounded on him. ‘The sun?’ he scoffed, with the bitter laugh of a man whose own faith is being sorely tested. ‘The sun has abandoned this place. We move by our own light, or not at all.’

And so we did. The sledges groaned, the dogs whined low in their throats, and we slid once more into the white, featureless throat of the world. There was no horizon, only a universal opalescence in which the sky and the ground were one. At times, the vast ice fields would buckle and break, throwing up pressure ridges like shattered bones, jagged and blue-green in the lantern light. We navigated these treacherous places with a slowness that was maddening, our progress a crawl, a scar upon the utter blankness. The world had become a study in gradations of white; the flat, dead white of the plains, the brilliant, crystalline white of the ice-fractures, the soft, suffocating white of the air itself. It was like travelling through the heart of a cataract, a slow, blinding journey to nowhere. The cold was a physical presence, a thing with teeth. It sought out the gaps in our clothing, the slightest exposure of skin, with a malevolent intelligence. It was not merely an absence of heat; it was an active, implacable force.

The lead guide, the one who had spoken of eating, moved at the head of our little convoy, a dark, solid shape in the swirling luminescence. He did not use a compass. He seemed to navigate by some other sense, by the feel of the ice under his feet, by the subtle texture of the wind, by a knowledge that was bred into his very bones. I watched him, fascinated. He was the only one of us who seemed to belong there, as at home in that desolation as a pilot in his harbour. The rest of us, with our scientific instruments and our tins of preserved food and our desperate belief in purpose, were the true ghosts, the unreal apparitions in that landscape. We were a fleeting, noisy dream in a long, silent reality.

Several hours passed in this spectral fashion. The only sounds were the hiss of the sledge runners, the panting of the dogs, and the occasional, sharp crack of the ice groaning like the hull of a dying ship. Then, it happened. It began, as these things often do, with a trifle. Jennings, the jumpy surveyor, let out a thin, reedy cry. ‘My tin!’ he shrieked, his voice cracking. ‘It’s gone! My tin of fruit!’ He had been hoarding a can of preserved peaches, a luxury he guarded with a jealousy that bordered on the pathological. He was clutching at his pack, his face, already pale, now a mask of pure, theatrical despair. ‘One of them took it!’ he screeched, pointing a trembling, mittened hand at the silent file of the guides. ‘I know it! The savages!’

Hargrove called a halt. The whole ridiculous procession stopped, a line of dark figures suspended in a universe of white. The guides stood motionless, their faces impassive in the glow of the lanterns. Hargrove strode over to Jennings, who was now sobbing, great, gulping, childish sobs. ‘Control yourself, man,’ Hargrove snapped, though his own eyes were darting nervously towards the guides. He was a man caught between the fatuous panic of his subordinate and the inscrutable silence of the natives, and his authority, already a flimsy thing, was visibly fraying. ‘What is this nonsense?’

‘He took it!’ Jennings insisted, jabbing his finger towards the youngest of the guides, a quiet boy who could not have been more than seventeen. ‘I saw him looking at it! They’re all starving, I tell you! They’ll murder us in our sleep for a biscuit!’

It was a tableau of sublime absurdity: a grown man, an agent of a great and powerful enterprise, having a hysterical fit over a can of peaches, while the vast, frozen continent watched with an indifference that was more terrifying than any malice. I looked at the boy he was accusing. The boy’s face was a calm, dark pool, betraying nothing, neither guilt nor innocence nor surprise. He simply stood, patient, waiting for the incomprehensible drama of the white men to play itself out. The lead guide had turned his head slightly, and his eyes, deep-set and ancient, met mine across the snow. There was no anger in them, only a profound, bottomless weariness, the weariness of a man who has witnessed the follies of a younger, shriller species a thousand times before.

‘There will be order,’ Hargrove declared, his voice a ludicrously small sound in the immense silence. ‘We will have a search.’ He seemed to think that order was a thing you could impose upon a continent’s indifference with a loud voice and a petty decree. He marched towards the guides, his posture a stiff parody of command. ‘Unpack your things,’ he ordered.

The lead guide said nothing. He did not move. He simply looked at Hargrove, and in his gaze there was a quality of stillness so absolute that it seemed to pull the heat from the air. The other guides followed his lead, remaining as immobile as the ice formations around us. They did not refuse, you understand; that would have been an act of defiance, a thing Hargrove could have understood and reacted to. Instead, they simply… were. They existed outside his command, beyond the reach of his authority. It was a passive resistance so total, so fundamental, that it made Hargrove’s blustering seem like the antics of a furious child beating his fists against a mountain.

Hargrove’s face, a florid, fleshy face, went from red to a mottled purple. ‘Do you hear me?’ he roared, the sound swallowed instantly by the snow. ‘I gave you an order!’ He took a step towards the lead guide, his hand reaching for the pistol at his belt.

It was then I stepped forward. ‘Hargrove,’ I said, and my own voice sounded strange to me, thin and distant. ‘Leave it be. It is a can of fruit.’

‘It is the principle!’ he hissed, his eyes wild. ‘It is discipline! Without it, we are lost!’

‘We are already lost, Hargrove,’ I said, more to myself than to him. I turned to the lead guide. I felt the absolute folly of my position, a translator between two languages that had no common root, the language of schedules and the language of silence. I looked at the man, at his face carved by wind and time, and I gestured towards Jennings, who was still snivelling. ‘He has lost his food,’ I said, using the few words of their tongue I had learned. ‘He is afraid.’

The guide looked not at me, but past me, at Jennings. He held that gaze for a long moment. Then, slowly, he reached into the folds of his own furs and produced a small, leather-wrapped parcel. He undid the thong and unfolded the leather, revealing a piece of dried meat, dark and hard as wood. It was, I knew, a piece of his own meagre ration, a thing more precious than gold in this wasteland. He held it out, not to Jennings, but to me. His expression did not change. It was not a gift; it was a statement. I took the piece of meat. It was cold and heavy in my hand.

I walked over to Jennings and held it out to him. ‘Here,’ I said. ‘Take this. And be quiet.’

Jennings stared at the piece of meat as if it were a venomous snake. ‘What is that? I won’t eat their filthy food!’ he cried.

‘Then starve,’ I said, my patience, a resource I had not even known I possessed, suddenly and completely exhausted. I turned my back on him and walked to where Hargrove stood, fuming and impotent. ‘The matter is settled,’ I said. ‘Let us move on.’

Hargrove looked from me to the silent guides, his face a mess of confusion and wounded pride. He wanted a confrontation, a clear act of mutiny he could crush. He had been denied it. He had been met instead with a quiet dignity that his mind could not process. Finally, with a snort of disgust, he gestured brusquely. ‘Proceed,’ he muttered. ‘Proceed.’

We packed up and the journey resumed, but the air between us had changed. It was no longer just cold; it was poisoned with suspicion and a quiet, simmering resentment. The bond of our shared purpose, fragile as it was, had been broken. The surveyors huddled closer together, casting fearful glances at the guides. And the guides… the guides had withdrawn into a place we could not reach. They performed their duties, yes, but mechanically, without the spark of life and intelligence they had shown before. Their restraint, the thing I had marvelled at, had not broken; it had solidified, turning from a principle of patience into a wall of ice.

The lead guide no longer looked at me. He had retreated behind his own eyes. I felt a sense of loss that was profound and irrational. It was as if a door to some ancient, vital knowledge had been shut in my face, locked by the petty foolishness of a man mourning a can of peaches. I still held the piece of meat he had given me. I did not eat it. I kept it in my pocket, where its hardness was a constant, solid reminder of the chasm that had opened between us. It was a strange sort of sacrament, a communion with a faith I had only just begun to perceive, and had now been excommunicated from.

Later that day, if day was the word for that perpetual, sourceless light, the ice began to change. It became thinner, and we could see the dark, impossibly black water moving sluggishly beneath it in places. The lead guide stopped. He stood for a long time, head cocked as if listening to something I could not hear. The other guides gathered behind him, their postures tense, alert. Hargrove slid up beside me, his breath pluming. ‘What now?’ he grumbled. ‘Why have we stopped?’

‘He is listening,’ I said.

‘Listening to what? The ice?’ he sneered.

The lead guide turned. For the first time since the incident with the tin, he looked directly at me. He spoke a single word, a word that was soft and guttural, yet it seemed to carry an immense weight. I did not understand it, but I understood its meaning. It meant: Wrong. It meant: End. He pointed not forward, but off to the west, a direction that diverged sharply from the route laid out on Hargrove’s map.

‘What did he say?’ Hargrove demanded.

‘He says the way forward is no good. He says we must go west.’

‘Nonsense,’ Hargrove snapped, pulling out his map and compass, the articles of his faith. ‘The objective is north-east. The map is clear. The company’s survey is clear. Tell him we go north-east.’

I conveyed this, feeling like a fool. The guide listened patiently. When I was finished, he did not argue. He did not protest. He simply gave a slight, almost imperceptible shake of his head. Then he turned his back on us, and, with the other guides following in a silent line, began to walk west, away from our sledges, away from our route, away from us. They did not run; they walked with a steady, deliberate pace, their dark forms shrinking against the vast whiteness. They were not deserting, not in the military sense of the word. They were simply leaving. They had their own path, their own knowledge, and we were no longer a part of it.

‘Stop!’ Hargrove screamed, his voice raw with panic. ‘Stop them! They are abandoning us!’ He drew his pistol, his hand shaking violently. ‘I will shoot them! I’ll shoot them down like dogs!’

But he did not shoot. We both knew, as did the surveyors who were staring, open-mouthed, that to shoot them would be to sign our own death warrant. They were our only link to survival in this place, and they had just severed it. We watched them go. We watched them until they were nothing but small, dark specks, and then the white, luminous air swallowed them completely.

We were alone. The four of us: Hargrove, myself, and the two remaining surveyors, Jennings and a quiet, haggard man named Croft. We were alone with our sledges, our frightened dogs, our tins of food, and our map, a piece of paper that suddenly seemed like the most useless and pathetic object in the entire universe. The silence returned, but it was a new kind of silence now. It was the silence of a tomb. The guides had not just taken their knowledge with them; they had taken the life of the landscape. Without them, the wilderness was no longer an inscrutable but living entity; it was simply a vast, dead thing, an endless, frozen shroud. And I wondered then, not for the last time, which of us was truly starving, and for what. We had our fill of beans and salted meat, but our souls were utterly famished, and out here, in the great, white emptiness, there was nothing, absolutely nothing, for them to eat.

All that remained was a vast, bottomless despair.

He seemed to look, not at me, but through me, at the civilization I represented, the world of rules and reports and sound methods that was reclaiming him.

His eyes were closed, but his lips moved, forming silent words. He was already gone, his mind adrift on a dark tide that was carrying him far away from me, from the river, from everything.

The jungle watched us pass, implacable and silent, having taken what it wanted and given back only a shell, a whisper, and a profound and terrible lesson.

It had only just begun.

They began firing wildly into the fog, a mad, senseless fusillade, their faces contorted with a kind of ecstatic terror. They blasted away at the white emptiness, at the phantoms of their own fear, making a prodigious noise, but hitting nothing, seeing nothing. The manager screamed at them to stop, to save the ammunition, but they were beyond reason.

My helmsman, a sturdy fellow from the coast, stood beside me, his body rigid, his eyes glued to the water just ahead of our bows. He was steering, and I was watching, our shared concentration a tiny island of purpose in the midst of the pandemonium. He grunted, and spun the wheel hard over. I saw it at the same moment: a black, jagged shape that broke the surface for a second, a dead tree hungry for our hull, before we slid past. He flashed me a grin, a brief, brilliant show of teeth in his black face. And in that instant, a long, wooden shaft, a spear, flew out of the mist. It did not fly so much as appear, a sudden, impossible line drawn through the air. I saw it strike him, just under the ribs. He let out no cry, only a soft, astonished gasp. His hands flew from the wheel, and he clutched at the spear, looking down at it with an expression of profound, uncomprehending surprise. He collapsed slowly, not falling so much as folding in on himself, and lay at my feet, his blood, shockingly red, pooling on the deck.

The spear shaft, which had broken off, got tangled in my feet. I was wading in his blood. The pilgrims were still firing, the noise a physical assault. I could feel the steamer beginning to turn, threatening to broach. With all my strength I fought the wheel, trying to keep her nose upstream. I could not bear the feeling, the warm, sticky wetness. It was a detail of an incredible, grotesque triviality, yet it filled my mind to the exclusion of all else. The danger, the arrows, the dying man at my feet, all of it receded before the pressing, urgent need for dry footwear.

The unseen enemy was stunned into stillness. I pulled the cord again, and then a third time, sending long, wailing blasts into the now-quiet mist. A moment later, the fog began to lift in earnest, not gently this time, but torn apart, ripped into great, swirling shreds by a wind that had sprung up from nowhere.

And in the centre of it all, a flagpole, from which hung a pitiful, unidentifiable rag. But what drew the eye, what held it in a sort of horrified fascination, were the posts. A series of slender posts, arranged in a semi-circle before the main hut, and on top of each post, a round, dark object. I raised my binoculars, my hands trembling slightly. He ran down to the water’s edge, shouting something we could not hear over the hiss of our steam. He was young, with a smooth, boyish face, but his eyes had a wild, feverish look, and his constant, agitated motion was that of a man at the very end of his tether.

We brought the steamer in, and he scrambled aboard before the gangplank was even properly down. He seized my hands, babbling. ‘You are English! I knew it! I have been waiting. Oh, the joy! The joy!’ He was, it turned out, a Russian, a wandering sailor who had stumbled into Kurtz’s domain and fallen under his spell. He was Kurtz’s last disciple.

‘He is a god!’ the man in motley declared, his eyes shining with a mad fervour. ‘You should have heard him. The ideas! The knowledge! He has enlarged my mind.’ He chattered on, a torrent of words about ivory, about the soul, about poetry, about the local tribes who adored Kurtz and for whom Kurtz would sometimes preside over ‘unspeakable rites.’ He explained the attack. ‘They don’t want him to go,’ he said, with a sort of simple pride. ‘It was I who warned you. He has been very ill. They fear you have come to take him away.’ And the heads? I asked him about the heads on the stakes. ‘Oh, those?’ he said, with a casual wave of his hand. ‘Those are rebels. It was a lesson. He had to be severe.’ He spoke of it as one might speak of pruning a rose bush.

Then they brought him out. They carried him on a makeshift stretcher, a gaunt, skeletal figure wrapped in blankets. But there was nothing of the invalid in his face. His head was bald as an ivory ball, his features emaciated, but his eyes burned with a feverish, consuming intensity. And the voice. It was a voice that seemed to come from a great depth, a resonant baritone that held you captive. ‘I am glad to see you,’ he said, and the words, though simple, were invested with a profound, almost royal, significance. The manager, all smiles and solicitude, fussed around him, but Kurtz’s eyes were fixed on me. In them I saw not gratitude, but a kind of searching, proprietary interest. I was a new audience, a fresh mind to be conquered.

We laid him in the little cabin that had been cleared for him, the one with the sliding shutter. The manager and I stood over him. The manager began to speak of the necessity of returning downriver at once, of the need for proper medical care. Kurtz listened, a faint, contemptuous smile playing on his lips. ‘I am not going,’ he said suddenly, his voice low but firm. ‘This is my station. My work is not finished.’ A flash of the old power, the indomitable will that had carved out a kingdom for itself in this desolation. The manager began to stammer about company orders, about responsibilities. Kurtz simply turned his head away, closing his eyes. The audience was over.

Later that day, as the sun began to sink, a figure appeared on the riverbank opposite the steamer. It was a woman. She was draped in dark cloths, adorned with brass leggings and bracelets, and her hair was built up in a fantastic, helmet-like coiffure. She was savage and superb, wild-eyed and magnificent; a tragic and monumental figure of sorrow and menace. She stood motionless, her hands raised in a gesture I could not interpret, and stared at the boat. The pilgrims gaped at her. The Russian whispered to me in an awed voice, ‘His woman. She helped him. She is a queen here.’ She did not utter a sound, but her presence was more powerful than any cry. It was a claim, a silent, unanswerable assertion of ownership. Kurtz belonged to her, to the jungle, to the darkness. Then, as the dusk deepened, she turned and walked away, vanishing back into the wall of trees as silently as she had appeared.

That night, I was woken by a sudden intuition of alarm. I went out on deck. The moon was up, casting a ghostly light on the river. I looked towards the cabin. The door was open. Kurtz was gone. A blind panic seized me. Not for him, but for the scandal, the complications, the report I would have to write. I grabbed a rifle and plunged ashore, following a trail in the dew-soaked grass. I found him not fifty yards from the circle of huts, crawling on his hands and knees. He was trying to get back to the fires, to the drums that had begun to beat softly in the distance, to the unspeakable rites. He saw me and rose unsteadily to his feet, a terrifying, spectral figure in the moonlight. For a moment I thought he would speak, would command me to go, would unleash some terrible power. But he was only a sick man. ‘You will be lost,’ I said, my voice sounding strange in my own ears. ‘Utterly lost.’ I spoke to him of his fame, of his name, of the great career that awaited him in Europe. I lied to him, with an eloquence I did not know I possessed, painting a picture of a world that I knew, and he knew, was a hollow sham. And he listened. Something in my words, some echo of that other life, reached him. He let me lead him back to the boat, his arm on my shoulder, a dead weight of bone and fever.

We started downriver the next morning. The journey was a slow, torturous crawl through a landscape of silent, brooding hostility. The wilderness that had consumed him seemed to be watching us go, reluctant to release its prize. And Kurtz lay in his cabin, dying. He spoke, in fits and starts, his voice now a reedy whisper, now a booming echo of its former power. He spoke of ivory, of his Intended, of the station, of the immense wealth he had gathered. ‘My ivory,’ he would murmur, his eyes gleaming. ‘My Intended, my station, my river.’ He had taken possession of it all, and it had taken possession of him. He gave me his papers, a chaotic bundle of documents, including the magnificent, rambling report he had written for the Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs. At the end of its seventeen pages of soaring rhetoric, he had scrawled a final, unsteady postscript: ‘Exterminate all the brutes!’

He faded day by day. The voice grew weaker, the fire in his eyes dimmed. He lay there, a husk, a vessel emptied of its dark energy. The steamer, as if in sympathy, broke down again, a petty failure of a minor steam-pipe. We were adrift, the current swinging us slowly, and the jungle waited. I spent my time in his cabin, an unwilling confessor to a soul in torment. He was lucid one moment, raving the next. He saw things in the dark corners of the tiny room, things that made him cry out. I would sit and watch him, the single candle between us casting our shadows, huge and distorted, on the wall behind. He seemed to be wrestling with something, some final, terrible knowledge. On the last evening, in the profound stillness of our anchorage, he seemed to rally. He looked at me, his gaze clear and steady for the first time in days. He was trying to speak. ‘I am lying here in the dark waiting for death,’ he whispered. I sat with him, the silence thickening around us, a silence broken only by his ragged breathing. The little cabin was a universe, a tomb. I watched the life ebb from him, a tide going out into a dark sea, and then, with a strength I would not have thought he possessed, he pushed himself up on one elbow, his eyes, wide and staring, fixed on something beyond me, beyond the flimsy wall of the cabin, beyond the night itself. He was seeing it, at last. The thing he had been seeking, the thing he had been fleeing, the thing he had become. His face was a mask of utter, comprehensive knowledge. And then he spoke, not in a whisper, but in a clear, resonant voice that seemed to fill the small cabin and the vast darkness beyond. ‘The horror!’ he said. ‘The horror!’

And then he was gone. The light, the knowledge, the terrible understanding, it all vanished from his face, leaving it a slack, empty mask. He fell back on the pillow, a faint sigh escaping his lips, a puff of air, a final, empty breath. The candle flickered, and for a moment, I thought it had gone out. But it was still there, a tiny, wavering point of light in the immense, overwhelming darkness. I sat there for a long time, the silence in the cabin now more profound than the silence of the jungle outside. The horror. He had said it. He had judged it. He had passed sentence. But on what? On his own life? On the wilderness? On the whole sorry, bloody business of our glorious enterprise? I did not know. But I knew that I had heard the cry of a soul that had seen the truth and could not bear it. And I knew that in his final, terrible moment of clarity, Kurtz had been more alive, more human, than all the rest of us put together.

I rose and went out on deck. The manager was there, silhouetted against the faint starlight. He turned as I approached, his face a pale oval in the gloom. ‘Is he dead?’ he asked, his voice carefully neutral, but I could hear the undercurrent of eagerness, of relief. ‘Yes,’ I said. ‘He is dead.’ He was silent for a moment. Then he said, ‘A great loss to the Company. A great loss.’ And he walked away, his shoulders a little squarer, his step a little lighter. He had what he wanted. The ivory was safe. The troublesome voice was silenced. The accounts could be balanced. I stood by the rail, looking out into the darkness. The world was still there, the river, the jungle, the stars. Nothing had changed. And yet, everything had changed. A voice had been stilled, a light had been extinguished, and I was alone with the memory of it, a memory that would be my companion for the rest of my days, a dark, secret knowledge that I could never share, never explain. I was the keeper of the horror. And as the first pale light of dawn began to creep into the eastern sky, and the engineers, with a final, triumphant clang, brought the engine back to life, I knew that the journey down the river was not over. It had only just begun.

In my delirium, I was back on the river, the fog thick around me, listening to a cry of infinite desolation. I saw Kurtz’s face, illuminated by a flickering candle, his eyes filled with a terrible, comprehensive knowledge. ‘The horror!’ His voice was the only solid thing in a world of shifting, nightmarish shapes.

The manager had already gone down to the coast, taking the ivory with him. I had delivered the goods.

The silence of the deep jungle had been a thing of awe, a silence that contained all the secrets of the beginning of the world. This silence, here, was different. It was the silence of a whited sepulchre, a silence filled with the unspoken lies and petty cruelties of men who called themselves civilized. I had thought the journey into the interior was a journey into darkness. I was wrong. The real journey, the long, slow journey through the rest of my days with this knowledge as my sole companion, had only just begun.

I said nothing. I kept my eyes on the river, on a submerged snag that created a treacherous, boiling eddy just ahead. He waited, expecting some sort of concurrence, some shared acknowledgement of the company’s misfortune. When none came, he cleared his throat and shifted his line of attack. ‘His end was… peaceful, I trust? He said nothing… of consequence?’ The question was delicately put, but his cold little eyes were sharp, probing. He wanted to know what secrets, if any, had been passed. He wanted to be sure the dead man’s accounts were closed in every sense.

‘He spoke,’ I said, my voice sounding rusty and unfamiliar to my own ears.

The manager leaned in slightly, a flicker of genuine, avaricious curiosity animating his fleshy features. ‘And?’

I looked at him then, at his clean collar, his neat little beard, his air of being utterly impervious to the vast, brooding wilderness that surrounded us and the deeper wilderness that Kurtz had explored. ‘He was disappointed in the administration,’ I said, with a kind of savage irony that was entirely lost on him. ‘He thought the Company was not living up to its noble ideals.’

A look of faint confusion, then of dawning comprehension, crossed his face. Ah, yes. Ideals. That was safe territory. ‘Ah! Yes. A man of high principles,’ he murmured, nodding sagely. ‘It preyed on his mind, no doubt. The climate, the isolation… it can affect even the strongest. We must make allowances. I shall make a note of it in my report. A most conscientious servant of the Company, to the very end.’ He patted my arm in a gesture of odious fellowship. ‘You have handled a difficult situation with great… discretion, Mr. Marlow. It will be remembered.’

He walked away, a man entirely content, leaving me with the taste of ashes in my mouth. A conscientious servant. Discretion. He had taken Kurtz’s immense, terrible despair and filed it away under a neat, bureaucratic heading. He had reduced ‘The horror!’ to a mere footnote in a ledger of profit and loss. And I had let him. I had given him a stone, a worthless bit of cant, when he had asked for the bread of Kurtz’s final truth. What else could I have done? Could I have told him? Could I have said, ‘He judged you, he judged me, he judged the whole rotten enterprise with his last breath’? He would have stared at me, then concluded I had a touch of the fever myself. He would have been right, in a way. I did have a fever, a fever of the soul, contracted in the stagnant air of Kurtz’s station.

We steamed on. The river, which on the way up had seemed a malevolent, living entity, a serpent leading us into a dark heart, was now just a river. A broad, muddy, indifferent waterway. The banks, which had seemed to watch us with a silent, brooding hostility, were now just banks: miles and miles of monotonous, tangled green. The spell was broken. Or rather, the spell had withdrawn, coiled back into itself, leaving behind a world that was merely dreary, shabby, and pointless. The silence was no longer profound and threatening; it was merely empty. We passed the spot where our helmsman had fallen, a spear in his side. One of the pilgrims pointed it out. ‘That’s where that black fellow copped it,’ he remarked, as one might point out a curious landmark. The helmsman was already a footnote, a minor incident in the grander narrative of their escape.

My own crew, the dark-skinned fellows from the coast, seemed to feel the change as well. The alert, watchful tension had gone out of them. They went about their duties with a listless, mechanical efficiency. The headman, my magnificent cannibal with the artfully arranged hair, no longer stood at the rail staring into the fog with pensive dignity. I saw him hunkered down with his companions, sharing one of those leaf-wrapped parcels of foul-looking dough. They were still hungry, no doubt, but the sharp, predatory edge was gone. The potential for a final, desperate act of consumption had passed. They had looked into the abyss alongside us, and what they had seen, or felt, I could not guess. But now, on the journey back, they were simply tired, underfed labourers, their own inscrutable secrets locked away behind their quiet, impassive faces. They had a restraint that was not of our world, a restraint that was perhaps older, deeper, and had nothing to do with farcical laws or the fear of consequences. It was simply there, an ancient, inherited wisdom of endurance. It made the pilgrims, with their frantic anxieties and their petty triumphs, seem like hysterical children.

We stopped once more for wood, at a clearing that looked as if it had been hacked out of the jungle with a dull knife and then abandoned in a hurry. The wood was stacked, ready for us. Another of Kurtz’s legacies, no doubt. Another trace of his furious, methodical energy. As the crew began to load the fuel, I saw something half-buried in the mud near the bank. It was a book. I scrambled down and pulled it out. It was a tattered copy of ‘An Inquiry into some Points of Seamanship,’ by a man named Tower, or Towson. It was water-stained and smeared with mud, but the text was still legible. It was a simple, practical manual, full of instructions on rigging, ballast, and the duties of a ship’s master. And in the margins, in a faint, spidery hand, were notes. Not in English. They looked like Cyrillic. Cipher, I thought at first, but then I realized it was simply another language.

I stood there, holding this absurdly out-of-place object, a technical manual annotated in Russian, found in the heart of an African jungle. It felt like a message from a ghost, a remnant of that other ghost who had haunted Kurtz’s station, the Russian, the harlequin, the boyish adventurer who had nursed Kurtz and worshipped his words. He had loved Kurtz, he had said. He had understood him. Or had he? Perhaps he had only understood the words, the magnificent flow of eloquence, without comprehending the darkness from which they sprang. He had been enchanted by the voice, and I had been left with its final, terrible echo. This book, with its straightforward, honest talk of chains and anchors, seemed suddenly like a relic of a saner world, a world where things had clear names and purposes. I tucked it into my coat, a strange, pathetic souvenir of my journey to the interior.

Days passed. They melted into one another, a monotonous sequence of glaring sun and humid, starless nights. The river broadened. We began to see signs of other stations, pathetic little clearings with a flag-pole and a corrugated iron shed, looking like outposts of some forgotten, half-hearted invasion. At one, a solitary white man, emaciated and yellow with fever, ran down to the bank, waving his arms. He was shouting, but his voice was too thin to carry over the churn of the paddles. The manager looked at him through his binoculars. ‘He seems distressed,’ he observed calmly. ‘Probably wants us to stop. No time. We have a schedule to keep. And the mail.’ He lowered the glasses and turned away. The man on the bank grew smaller and smaller, a frantic, stick-like figure of despair, swallowed up by the immense green indifference of the landscape. We left him there, another soul being slowly digested by the wilderness.

I felt my own health beginning to fail. The ‘little fever’ I had carried for so long began to assert itself. There were times when the familiar deck of the steamboat seemed to heave and tilt in a most unseamanlike manner, when the faces of the pilgrims wavered before my eyes like shapes seen through heated air. The jungle on either side would sometimes seem to pulse with a silent, malevolent energy, its greens becoming lurid and venomous. Kurtz’s last words began to detach themselves from their context, to float freely in my mind. ‘The horror! The horror!’ The phrase would surface without warning, a bubble of pure dread rising from the depths of my memory. It was no longer just his judgment; it was becoming my own. I saw it in the rapacious gleam in the pilgrims’ eyes as they checked the ivory lashings; I saw it in the manager’s smooth, self-satisfied smile; I saw it in the blank, uncomprehending face of the continent itself.

He was carrying a tin plate on which lay a biscuit and a piece of tinned meat. A peace offering, perhaps. He had a look of sanctimonious gravity on his face. ‘A terrible loss, Mr. Kurtz,’ he said, sighing. ‘But a judgment, I think. A judgment on his methods. He had no restraint. He consorted with… savages. He forgot his station. The Almighty does not suffer such pride to go unpunished.’

I looked at his earnest, foolish face, at the pink pyjamas still peeking out from under his trousers, and a wave of profound, weary disgust washed over me. This creature, this animated bundle of greed and platitudes, was passing judgment on Kurtz. Kurtz, who had at least had the courage to look into the abyss. This man would not even dare to look into his own soul. I thought of Kurtz’s magnificent, soaring rhetoric, his talk of light, and pity, and progress, and then I thought of his final, whispered verdict. He had at least been honest in the end. These men, they were a walking, breathing lie. ‘Yes,’ I said. ‘A judgment.’ My agreement seemed to satisfy him. He nodded, pleased at this confirmation of his own petty theology, and left me to my fever and my thoughts.

We arrived at the Central Station in a downpour. Not a cleansing, tropical torrent, but a mean, persistent drizzle that turned the trampled red earth into a slick, greasy mud. The place was exactly as I had left it: a scene of aimless activity and organized decay. The same faces, a little more sallow, a little more gaunt, came out to greet us. The chief accountant, still immaculate in his starched collar, emerged from his office to oversee the unloading of the ivory. He did not ask about Kurtz the man, only about Kurtz the agent. ‘I trust his accounts were in order?’ he asked me, his pen poised over a ledger.

‘They are in the care of the manager,’ I said, turning away.

The journey was over. I had brought the ivory back. I had brought back the story of a man’s soul. They cared only for the ivory. I was left with the soul. I was ill, profoundly ill. The company doctor took one look at me and shook his head. They put me in a clean, bare room, and for weeks I hovered in a grey limbo between life and death. The fever burned away the last of my physical strength, but it could not touch the core of my memory. In my delirium, I was back on the river, the fog thick around me, listening to a cry of infinite desolation. I saw Kurtz’s face, illuminated by a flickering candle, his eyes filled with a terrible, comprehensive knowledge. ‘The horror!’ His voice was the only solid thing in a world of shifting, nightmarish shapes.

Slowly, I began to mend. I was a great disappointment to the doctor, who had predicted my demise with a certain professional satisfaction. I crawled back into the world of the living, or what passed for it in that place. I was thin, wasted, a scarecrow of a man, but I was alive. The manager had already gone down to the coast, taking the ivory with him. He had left a message for me, a formal note thanking me for my services and informing me that the Company viewed my conduct in a most favourable light. I was a success. I had not died. I had delivered the goods.

But as I sat on the verandah of my quarters, looking out at the pointless bustle of the station, at the listless black men in chains and the sallow-faced agents with their furtive, greedy eyes, I felt no triumph. The silence of the deep jungle had been a thing of awe, a silence that contained all the secrets of the beginning of the world. This silence, here, was different. It was the silence of a whited sepulchre, a silence filled with the unspoken lies and petty cruelties of men who called themselves civilized. I had thought the journey into the interior was a journey into darkness. I was wrong. The darkness was here, in the bright, pitiless glare of the station, in the neat columns of the ledgers, in the hollow words of piety and progress. Kurtz had tried to master the darkness, and it had consumed him. These men did not even see it. They carried it within them, an integral part of their being, and called it civilization. And I knew, with a certainty that chilled me more than any fever, that while the river journey was over, the darkness had only just found its true home, not in the heart of a continent, but in the heart of a man who had looked into it and brought a piece of it back with him. The real journey, the long, slow journey through the rest of my days with this knowledge as my sole companion, had only just begun.

I folded the report carefully and put it away. This was not a thing for the world to see. The world could not understand. It would see only the madness, not the terrible, agonizing logic that had led to it.

The sepulchral city, when I finally reached it, was just as I remembered it: a place of hushed streets, of tall, narrow houses that looked like tombs, of people who moved with a quiet, self-satisfied gravity. He wrung my hand and said that I had helped to secure a great man’s legacy. I had. I had helped to build the lie, to whitewash the sepulchre. It was, I told myself, what Kurtz would have wanted. He had judged himself, but he had not wanted the world to judge him. He had wanted the idea of himself to survive, pure and unsullied.

And then there was the last, the hardest, duty. I went to see his Intended. I had her address, on a street that was a canyon of tall, dark houses. The air was heavy with the scent of wealth and mourning. The house was a tomb, a place of shadows and hushed reverence. To turn back now, after so much, was unthinkable. It was not a matter of duty, not anymore. It was a necessity of the soul. I had to see it through to the end. I had to know.

The change was breathtakingly swift. One moment we were in a shroud; the next, the river was there, a broad, coppery ribbon, and the jungle rose on either side, immense and silent.
